How Developer-First Marketing Turned Bank Plumbing Into a Trusted Brand Volodymyr Khomichenko 6 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size In January 2021, a founder logged into Zoom to deliver the worst news of his career. His name was Zach Perret, co-founder of Plaid. For months, his employees had mentally spent money that wasn’t theirs yet — a $5.3 billion acquisition by Visa was supposed to close any day. Some had already picked out houses. Some had already planned to quit. Then the U.S. Department of Justice sued to block the merger. Regulators didn’t describe Plaid as just another startup. They called it a “volcano” — something that looked quiet on the surface but was sitting on enormous, disruptive pressure underneath. They were right. But not in the way anyone expected. Nine months later, Plaid was worth $13.4 billion. More than double what Visa had offered. The failed deal didn’t kill the company — it set it free. This is the story of how that happened, and why the real engine behind Plaid’s rise wasn’t its technology. It was how they sold it. ▶️Listen to this episode [ Apple Podcasts ] [ YouTube ] Banking Before Plaid Felt Like the 1990s Rewind to 2012. Instagram had just sold to Facebook for a billion dollars. Smartphones were everywhere. And yet, if you wanted to link your bank account to an app, you’d wait three days for two tiny “verification” deposits to land in your account. If you wanted a loan, you walked into a branch. Financial infrastructure hadn’t caught up to the internet. Plaid’s founders, Zach Perret and William Hockey, weren’t trying to fix this. They were ex-consultants who spent their evenings at a climbing gym, dreaming up consumer finance apps. They built roughly seven different versions of a personal budgeting tool. All of them flopped — for the same reason. Nobody wants an app that scolds them for buying coffee. You don’t change your habits. You delete the app. The Real Product Was Hiding the Whole Time Here’s the part that actually mattered: while building those failed apps, Perret and Hockey noticed something strange. Ninety percent of their time wasn’t spent designing features. It was spent just trying to pull basic account data out of banks. There was no clean way to do it. No APIs. No shortcuts. Then a friend building Venmo said something that changed everything: “Your app is mediocre, but I’d pay to use whatever you built to connect to banks.” That was the real business. Not budgeting. Plumbing. Nobody wanted a smarter way to track spending. Everybody building fintech needed a faster way to access financial data. Winning Through Sheer Stubbornness Turning that insight into a company meant connecting to thousands of banks — most of which had no interest in cooperating. Early on, this meant building “screen scrapers”: bots that logged into a user’s bank account on their behalf just to pull balance data. It was messy, fragile, unglamorous work. They built over 12,000 of these integrations. One at a time. For an entire year, the company ran on just $60,000, raised from three separate angel investors — who all happened to be named Justin — after a larger funding round collapsed when the lead investor got cold feet about fintech. There was no shortcut. Just persistence. By 2016, early customers like Robinhood and Venmo started exploding in popularity, and every new user of those apps created a new Plaid connection behind the scenes. Growth stopped being something Plaid chased and started being something that happened automatically. Eventually, Plaid outgrew “connectivity” entirely. Today, with access to data from roughly one in three American bank account holders, it powers fraud detection, real-time credit scoring, and instant payments — a shift from being plumbing to being an analytics layer for the entire financial system. The Marketing Move Nobody Else Was Making Here’s where it gets interesting, and where most of the “how Plaid grew” narrative usually gets skipped. Plaid didn’t win with a killer sales team. It won by ignoring sales entirely — and going straight to the people writing the code. Talking to the Engineer, Not the Executive In 2013, the idea that a 24-year-old developer could choose your company’s core financial infrastructure was almost laughable. Most vendors sold to VPs and directors. Plaid bet on the developer instead. They put their entire API documentation online, publicly, with no sales call required. While competitors were still using clunky SOAP protocols, Plaid built clean REST APIs that felt modern and easy to integrate. Instead of account managers, Plaid hired engineers to talk to other engineers — in the same language, with the same priorities. Building a Market That Didn’t Exist Yet There’s a detail that’s easy to miss: when Plaid started, the word “fintech” barely existed as a category. Most investors didn’t believe there was a real market there at all. So Plaid didn’t just market a product — they had to manufacture belief in an entire industry.
